# Track 1 — observation and action schema

*Generated by `usvnav docs` from usvnav 0.1.0. Do not edit; edit the code.*

This is where the numbers live. The problem statement carries the task, the meaning of each field and the warnings that change how an agent is designed; this document carries every dtype, shape, range, sentinel and constant, and `docs/examples/` carries one real observation per condition captured from the scoring loop. If a number here disagrees with the statement, this document is right.

The interface, in full:

```python
class Agent:
    def __init__(self, config_path): ...      # once per process; a path inside your submission
    def reset(self, meta): ...                # once per episode; clear all state here
    def act(self, obs) -> [v_cmd, w_cmd]: ... # every tick, 10 Hz simulated time
```

No state may carry from one episode to the next; `reset` is where it is cleared. There is no end-of-episode callback: scoring learns nothing, so there is nothing to tell you.

## 1. Units, frames and signs

SI units throughout: metres, seconds, radians. Every angle in every array is in radians and wrapped to (−π, π].

**World frame:** right-handed 2D, `+x` along the reach's long axis, `+y` 90° counter-clockwise from it; heading ψ is measured counter-clockwise from `+x` to the bow.

**Body frame:** origin at the hull rectangle's centre, `+x` through the bow, `+y` to **port**. A positive `w_cmd`, a positive yaw rate, a positive bearing and a LiDAR beam index increasing from the bow all mean the same direction: **to port, counter-clockwise seen from above**. Under this convention "obstacle at beam 30 → bearing +60° → steer positive" turns *toward* it, which is the trap the convention exists to make visible.

**Raster mapping** (`bow_up`): a body-frame point `(x_b, y_b)` lands at `row = 100.0 − x_b / 0.5`, `col = 100.0 − y_b / 0.5` in continuous pixel coordinates, so the hull centre sits on the corner shared by the four central pixels, the bow points to row 0, and port is to the *left* of the image (a point 10 m ahead and 10 m to port lands upper-left).

## 2. Episode start — `reset(meta)`

`meta` is a dict. It is identical in all four conditions and carries **no obstacle geometry**: perceiving the surroundings is the task.

| key | type | example | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `boundary` | `float64` N×2 (here N = 33) | `[141.22, 37.72]` … | the navigable polygon in world metres — the shoreline. Water inside, bank outside; any part of the hull crossing it ends the episode as `out_of_bounds` |
| `waypoints` | `float64` K×2 (here K = 8) | `[204.34, 97.65]` … | the full ordered chain in world metres, to be reached **in order** |
| `arrival_radii` | `float64` K | `[5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0, …]` | metres; reaching waypoint k means the hull **centre** comes within radius k. Intermediate waypoints 5 m, the goal 3 m |
| `hull` | `(float, float)` | `(3.0, 2.0)` | length and width in metres. **A constant** — 3.0 × 2.0 m in every episode and every condition; it is listed for completeness, not because it varies |
| `observation_mode` | `str` | `'1-1'` | one of `1-1`, `1-2`, `1-3`, `1-4`; fixed for the episode and decides the type of `obs["perception"]` |

The start is stationary, at the departure berth, heading aligned with the first leg plus a per-episode offset of up to ±30°. Courses have 2–10 waypoints on legs of 40–160 m; a course may run down the reach and back, with its goal beside its start.

## 3. The action — `act(obs) -> [v_cmd, w_cmd]`

Two numbers, in any array-like of length 2: a **surge setpoint** in m/s and a **yaw-rate setpoint** in rad/s. They are setpoints, not forces: an autopilot turns them into thrust for the vessel, which is **Track 2's public nominal model** (`usvnav/plant.py`: a planar rigid body with linear damping, a stern azimuth thruster and a bow thruster). The hull has inertia and slips: a turn pushes the stern sideways, a hard turn at speed bleeds speed because the stern thruster's thrust is shared between surge and turning, the yaw rate you can have falls as speed rises, and a lower speed setpoint throttles back and coasts rather than braking — only a negative `v_cmd` reverses.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| `v_cmd` range | [-0.5, 2.0] m/s; cruise 1.5 m/s |
| `w_cmd` range | [−0.6, 0.6] rad/s |
| slew limits, applied by the simulator | 0.5 m/s and 0.3 rad/s per tick |
| vessel | 250 kg, damping X_u 200 / Y_v 300 N·s/m, N_r 900 N·m·s; stern 400 N (reverse 40 %), bow 150 N, arm 1.2 m |
| what a hard turn at full speed does | about 1.6 m/s and 0.5 rad/s, the hull slipping ~10° |
| control period | 0.1 s (10 Hz), simulated — the runner waits for `act` |
| out-of-range but finite | clipped to the range; the episode continues; `prev_action` shows the clipped value next tick |
| NaN, ±inf, wrong shape, exception | ends the episode as `invalid_action` / `crash`, a submission fault |

The 1-4 disturbance enters as a **lateral drift with no yaw moment**, so turn authority is untouched by it; holding a straight course at cruise against the maximum drift needs about a 13° crab angle.

## 4. Common observation fields

`obs` is a dict of named numpy arrays — never a flat vector. These six keys are present, with these types, in every condition. Real values are `float32`; the simulator integrates in `float64` and rounds on emission.

| field | dtype | shape | example (1-4, tick 120) | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `t` | `int32` | scalar | `120` | control tick since `reset`, 0-based; the time limit (§6) is in the same unit |
| `pose` | `float32` | 3 | `[84.251, 74.739, 0.190]` | `x, y` in world metres and heading ψ in radians, wrapped — your GNSS and compass |
| `vel` | `float32` | 3 | `[0.832, 0.223, -0.001]` | surge `u`, sway `v` (m/s, **over ground, body axes**) and yaw rate `r` (rad/s). `v` is the hull's slip: nonzero whenever it turns, in every condition, and under 1-4 it also carries the disturbance |
| `wp_index` | `int32` | scalar | `0` | index into `meta["waypoints"]` of the waypoint you are heading for now |
| `wp_polar` | `float32` | 2 | `[122.258, -0.001]` | distance in metres and **bow-relative bearing** in radians to that waypoint, wrapped; positive is to port. Redundant with `pose` and supplied so nobody re-implements the wrap |
| `prev_action` | `float32` | 2 | `[0.900, -0.001]` | the command **actually applied** last tick — after clipping — which can differ from what you returned. `[0, 0]` at `t = 0` |

Deliberately absent: obstacle information of any kind (that is `perception`), the disturbance state, remaining time (compute it from `t`), and any success or failure flag.

## 5. `obs["perception"]`, per condition

Sensing range is 50 m. For 1-3 that is a radius; for 1-1, 1-2 and 1-4 it is the half-width of a 100 × 100 m square centred on the hull, which reaches 70.71 m into its corners. Every observation is exact: no sensor noise, and the scoring renderer adds no noise (renderer noise exists only as an option you switch on yourself in the studio or with `--noise`, see 5.2).

### 5.1 Condition 1-1 — structured object list

A dict of fixed-length arrays with a validity mask, capacity 96, rows **nearest first**, zero-padded. A body is listed when its footprint intersects the observation square. Occluded bodies are listed — there is no visibility test.

| key | dtype | shape | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `valid` | `bool` | 96 | row `i` is a body; rows after the last valid one are zero padding |
| `cls` | `int8` | 96 | object class id, table below |
| `primitive` | `int8` | 96 | 0 = circle, 1 = oriented rectangle |
| `pos` | `float32` | 96×2 | body centre in the **body frame**, metres: `+x` ahead, `+y` to port |
| `heading` | `float32` | 96 | the body's heading relative to yours, radians, wrapped (0 for a circle) |
| `vel` | `float32` | 96×2 | the body's **over-ground** velocity, components in **your** axes, m/s. Static bodies are exactly `[0, 0]`; subtract your own `vel[:2]` for relative velocity |
| `extent` | `float32` | 96×2 | `(length, width)` in metres; a circle carries `(diameter, diameter)` |

| `cls` | class | primitive | size | moves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `buoy` | circle | 0.6 m diameter, fixed | no |
| 1 | `pier` | rectangle | 8–20 m × 4–10 m | no |
| 2 | `moored_vessel` | rectangle | 10–40 m × 3–10 m | no |
| 3 | `moving_vessel` | rectangle | 3–20 m × 1.2–6 m | yes, on a **lane** — a fixed path between two berths or end caps, run on a schedule (open lanes: one vessel every headway; closed lanes circulate) at 0.5–2.5 m/s, a pure function of time (§9); it does not react to you |
| 4 | `dock` | rectangle | 10–30 m × 5–15 m | no |

**The bank is not in the list**. `meta["boundary"]` already gives the shoreline exactly, so a row for it would carry nothing — but it means an agent driving on the object list alone drives ashore unless it puts the boundary in itself. 1-3's ray cast hits the bank and 1-2 draws it; 1-1 does not contain it. The example dump has 15 valid rows.

### 5.2 Condition 1-2 — top-view picture

A `uint8` array of shape 200×200×3: rows × columns × RGB, 0.5 m per pixel, 100 m across, `bow_up` — the bow points to row 0 and the whole scene rotates with you, so consecutive frames are mutually rotated by your yaw and `vel[2]` is what pays for compensating that. The ego hull is drawn. **Nothing occludes anything**: every body inside the square is drawn whole, whatever stands in front of it.

**The raster is the studio's picture.** It is drawn by the same code that draws the map in `usvnav studio` and `usvnav view` (`usvnav/look.py`), so what you see there is what the agent receives — not a flat class map. The base colours, exact sRGB:

| class | hex | RGB | appears in a 1-2 raster? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unobserved` | #000000 | (0, 0, 0) | no — it has no source in Track 1 |
| `water` | #16303B | (22, 48, 59) | yes |
| `dock` | #6B4F35 | (107, 79, 53) | yes |
| `pier` | #7E7B73 | (126, 123, 115) | yes (also rocks) |
| `bank` | #77725C | (119, 114, 92) | yes — outside the boundary polygon |
| `vessel` | #53606B | (83, 96, 107) | yes — moored **and** moving vessels share it; telling them apart is 1-2's task, not the palette's |
| `ego` | #F26E7A | (242, 110, 122) | yes — your own hull |
| `buoy` | #F0C820 | (240, 200, 32) | yes |

`outside_world` is in the shared ten-class vocabulary and has **no colour** here: generated terrain extends past the raster's 70.71 m corner reach, so it can never be painted; if it ever had to be, the renderer raises rather than substituting.

**What is drawn on top of the base colours**, all of it deterministic and stated in metres (`usvnav/look.py`): a wet band 2.5 m into the bank and a shallow band 3.5 m into the water along every shoreline; a drop shadow 0.6 m down-right of every body; a lighter deck panel inset 1.2 m on piers, vessels and docks; and an outline 0.2 m thick around every body in a darker tone (a ring outside the footprint for buoys and your own hull). The picture is painted at 0.25 m/px and box-downsampled 2× to 0.5 m/px, so edges are anti-aliased. Inside a class the colour is flat: the base colour exactly. Segment it as you would any picture — the base colours are the anchors; expect outline, shadow, shoreline and anti-aliased edge tones that are not in the table. `usvnav observe` writes the frame at any tick; the studio shows it beside the map it was drawn from.

**Noise is yours to add.** The scorer renders with no noise at all: the picture above is what a submission is scored on. Renderer noise is an exercise you set yourself — Track 2's renders carry noise; here the tooling lets you add your own and test against it. A noise function has the shape `(class_name, x_world, y_world) -> offsets`: the class being painted, the world coordinates of every pixel centre in metres, and integer offsets added to that class's base colour. Hand it to `RasterConfig.noise`, to `usvnav run|observe|view --noise module:function`, or pick it in the studio's *noise* selector, which applies it to every run the studio starts and to *What the agent saw*; the studio's work folder gets a `noise.py` to write them in. The kit ships one example, `usvnav.look.grain` (`--noise grain`): value noise of ±4 levels in 0.6 m blocks on water, ±11 levels in 1.0 m blocks on bank, ±6 levels in 0.4 m blocks on pier, ±5 levels in 0.4 m blocks on vessel, ±9 levels in 0.4 m blocks on dock, anchored to the world so it moves with the scene.

Bodies smaller than 2.0 px are drawn at 2.0 px, so a 0.6 m buoy paints as 1.0 m and is never missing, while collision and the 1-1 list keep its true size: a conservative agent gives it 0.2 m more room than it needs.

A rule-based classifier is enough for this picture — the classes are a handful of known colours, drawn without noise — and what 1-2 is testing is what comes after: objects carry no velocity and no identity, so a moving vessel is found by **associating it across frames** that your own rotation has moved, at about 0.3–0.5 px per tick.

In the example dump, pixels carrying a base colour exactly: `water` 26202, `pier` 378, `bank` 5460, `vessel` 198, `ego` 24, `buoy` 10; the other 7728 of 40000 carry shoreline, shadow, deck, outline or anti-aliased edge tones.

### 5.3 Condition 1-3 — planar LiDAR

A `float32` array of 180 ranges in metres. Beam `i` points at bearing `i · 2π/180` rad from the bow, **increasing to port** — 2° spacing over the full 360°, so beam 45 is abeam to port and beam 135 to starboard. First return only, so **this is the one condition with occlusion**: a body behind another is not reported. Single planar cast, no mount height — the world has no vertical dimension.

**No return is `50.0`, the maximum range — never `0`.** A zero would be indistinguishable from a surface at zero distance, and any agent that judges danger by the array's minimum would read open water as an imminent collision. The bank returns beams like any surface.

Example dump: min 20.30 m at beam 121, 77 of 180 beams with no return.

### 5.4 Condition 1-4 — the raster, under a disturbance

`perception` is exactly 1-2's raster. What changes is the plant: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck drift in the **world frame** with correlation time τ = 20 s, bounded so the induced lateral speed never exceeds 0.35 m/s. It is smooth and mean-reverting, changes meaningfully over about τ — many times in one run — and is **not** in the observation: you see it as the mismatch between heading and course, which is `vel[1]` — the sway component, on top of the slip your own turns produce (which is there in every condition). In the example dump at tick 120, `vel` is `[0.832, 0.223, -0.001]` against `[0.900, -0.000, 0.000]` under 1-2 on the same course at the same tick.

The generator (`usvnav.plant.OUDisturbance`) ships; hidden episodes use unseen seeds of the same family.

## 6. How an episode ends, and the time limit

| outcome | tier | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `goal` | navigational | every waypoint reached in order, the hull centre inside the goal radius on the last one |
| `static_collision` | navigational | footprint intersection with a buoy, pier, moored vessel or dock, tested every tick |
| `dynamic_collision` | navigational | footprint intersection with a moving vessel |
| `out_of_bounds` | navigational | **any part** of the hull outside the boundary polygon — the shoreline; there is no separate grounding |
| `timeout` | navigational | `t` reached the limit without a collision or leaving the boundary |
| `crash` | submission fault | `reset` or `act` raised |
| `invalid_action` | submission fault | a non-finite or malformed action |
| `time_overrun` | submission fault | the episode's wall-clock limit ran out — 120 s from the `reset` call, the agent's time and the scorer's together; or `Agent(config_path)` past its time limit (RULES.md §4) |

**Time limit: 6000 ticks** (600 s simulated), one constant for every course. A run still afloat and untouched at the limit ends as `timeout`; the run record keeps how many waypoints it reached.

Within one tick the checks run in a fixed order so a re-run reproduces the outcome: submission fault → collision → out-of-bounds → goal → timeout.

**Clearance**, as the simulator measures it: per tick, the minimum surface-to-surface distance from the hull rectangle to any body **or the bank**, capped at 10 m; the episode statistic is the mean of the lowest 5% of those per-tick minima. Open water you happened to cross cannot raise it.

## 7. What the courses contain

A course is a stretch of river with a shoreline, a start pose, a chain of 2–10 waypoints on legs of 40–160 m — across the width, and out and back with the goal beside the start — static bodies of the classes in §5.1 with the sizes given there, and moving vessels on lanes (§9). The world is a 400 × 150 m box; the channel is 40–120 m wide. What an agent has to handle is the capability list in `docs/RULES.md` §1; no passage on a hidden route is narrower than 4 m, two hull widths.

The practice courses in `sets/practice/` are a few composite courses of low-to-medium difficulty. They show the format and the feel of a course, not the range of what the hidden set contains; the courses you test against are the ones you author in the editor or write as files (§9). Every hidden course passes the same course-file rules the studio and `usvnav validate` apply. No competent agent is distributed; the shipped tutorial agent usually fails.

## 8. The example dumps (`docs/examples/`)

One course (`course.json`), its `meta.json`, and the observation at tick 120 under each condition, driven there by the shipped tutorial agent and captured from `sim.run_episode` itself:

- `observation-1-1.json` — the six common fields and the full object list, padding included;
- `observation-1-2.png` — the raster, pixel-exact (open it with any image library; the `-x3` copy is upscaled by nearest neighbour for looking at); `observation-1-2.json` — the common fields and the per-class pixel counts;
- `observation-1-3.json` — the common fields and the 180 ranges;
- `observation-1-4.json` / `.png` — the same, under the disturbance: compare `vel` and `pose` with 1-2's.

Regenerate everything with `usvnav docs`; `usvnav observe COURSE --condition C` writes a single tick of your own.

## 9. The course file (`usvnav-course/2`)

Everything the studio, `usvnav validate`, `usvnav run` and the scorer read is one JSON file; the practice courses and `docs/examples/course.json` are examples. Metres and radians, `+x` along the reach, `+y` to port; coordinates are written to four decimals, and the file — not the object that produced it — is what runs. The editor writes it, and you can write it yourself:

```
{"format": "usvnav-course/2",
 "world": {"boundary": [[x, y], ...]},                 the navigable polygon; water at the box's x-edges is an end cap
 "start": {"x": .., "y": .., "heading_rad": ..},
 "waypoints": [{"x": .., "y": .., "arrival_radius_m": 5.0}, ..., {"..": .., "arrival_radius_m": 3.0}],
 "bodies": [{"class": "buoy", "primitive": "circle", "x": .., "y": .., "diameter_m": 0.6},
            {"class": "pier" | "moored_vessel" | "dock", "primitive": "rect", "x": .., "y": .., "length_m": .., "width_m": .., "heading_rad": ..}],
 "traffic": [],                                            legacy closed loops (class, length_m, width_m, speed_mps, phase_m, route); lanes replace them
 "lanes": [{"class": "moving_vessel", "closed": false,
            "route": [[x0, y0], [x1, y1], ...],              the path, 2 or more points (a closed lane 3 or more)
            "speeds_mps": [v0, v1, ...],                      one speed per route point, linear in between
            "headway_s": 45.0, "offset_s": 0.0,             open lanes: a vessel enters at route[0] every headway_s seconds, shifted by offset_s
            "vessels": [{"length_m": 12, "width_m": 3}, ...]}]}  the sizes the vessels cycle through
```

**Lanes** are how vessels move. An *open* lane's vessels appear at its first point on the schedule, run the route at the speeds given, and leave at its last point; both ends should sit on a *spawn wall* — an end cap (the water's edge at the world box) or a **berth**, a slip cut into the shoreline polygon — so a vessel is never seen appearing on open water. A *closed* lane's vessels circulate, spaced equally in time (no `headway_s`). Every pose is a pure function of time, so a run is reproducible and a vessel never reacts to you. `waypoints`: 2–10, legs 40–160 m, intermediate radius 5 m and the goal 3 m.

**What `usvnav validate FILE` (and the studio, on every save) checks about lanes** — each problem names its rule (below) and says what to change:

- L1 the corridor (the widest vessel plus 0.5 m each side) is clear of bodies and of the shore;
- L2 speeds within 0.5–2.5 m/s, acceleration between points at most 0.2 m/s²;
- L3/L4 the spacing guarantee: at the speed where your route meets the lane, `headway · v − L ≥ 7 m` (room for the hull between two vessels), and at every passage too narrow to pass beside a vessel the headway leaves time to get through at 0.75 m/s — so a lane can always be crossed by waiting for the gap;
- L5 lanes do not touch each other; L7 the corridor keeps out of the start pose and the goal's disc; L8 no lane vessel within 50 m of the start at t = 0;
- L9 vessels 3–20 m × 1.2–6 m and a metre narrower than the lane's tightest passage; L11 no turn over 60° at a route point (insert points to round a corner); L10 (a warning) an open lane that does not end on a spawn wall.

Static bodies follow the sizes in §5.1, keep off the start pose and every arrival disc, and must leave the route connected through free water for the hull. The other rules are named by what they check: `shoreline` (the boundary is a simple polygon), `reach` (the navigable area stays inside the world box; a warning), `terrain` (a file's terrain extent covers the raster's reach), `start` (the start pose is inside the boundary and touches nothing), `waypoints` (their count and leg lengths), `radius` (the arrival radii; a warning), `keep-clear` (no body inside the start pose or an arrival disc), `size` (body sizes per class; a warning), `connected` (each leg is passable through free water), and `traffic` / `traffic-speed` for legacy loops. The editor's own checks are the subset that needs no free-space grid; the studio's save and `usvnav validate` run the whole list.
